comments.name: MARK B PACKER

The ineffectiveness of warnings constitutes one of the central pillars of Western thought.  Think of Cassandra. But most striking for me is that opening scene in Act II of Wagner's Siegfried,  when Wotan, posing as the Wanderer,  and Alberich, his nemesis, both try to warn Fafner, who has transformed himself into a supposedly invincible dragon to protect his gold hoard,  that his life is in danger because of the approaching young hero Siegfried. Fafner replies, dragon-voiced: "I'm hungry for him." 

At which critical turning point in the mighty Ring  drama Wotan intones, to the musical theme of the Twilight of the Gods: "Alles ist nach seiner Art. An ihr wirst du nichrts aendern."  Translation: " Everything goes after its own fashion, you can't do a thing to change its course."

So, are we stuck with that dire fate, economic and then social collapse?  Supposedly not; after some panic, wiser heads will emerge and prevail , and effectuate the tough choices  necessary to rectify the crisis.  Any bets on this? I understand that betting platforms are all the rage nowadays.

(Part 1) 
A nine-year-old boy was bitten fourteen times by a rabid dog, his mother refused to let him die.
It was Independence Day, 1885.

Joseph Meister was nine years old, walking through his village in Alsace, France, when the dog hit him from behind. No warning. No time to run. The animal was rabid, and before anyone could pull it off, it had torn into him fourteen times. 

His hands. His legs. His thighs. A bystander finally drove the dog away with an iron bar. The animal was killed immediately. The rabies confirmed shortly after.

In 1885, that confirmation meant one thing.
Death.

Once the virus reached the brain, nothing on earth could intervene. The progression was merciless, paralysis creeping through the body, violent convulsions, an unbearable and uncontrollable terror of water. No human being in recorded history had ever survived rabies once it fully took hold. Doctors had no treatment to offer. Families had no choice but to watch. You simply waited for the end to arrive.

Joseph's mother, Marie-Angélique, was not going to wait.
She had heard something, a rumor, thin and secondhand, about a scientist working in Paris. Not a doctor. A chemist. Someone who had reportedly developed something that stopped rabies in dogs. No human had ever received it. Nobody knew if it would work on a child. Nobody knew if it might kill him faster than the disease itself.

She wrapped her son's wounds, put him on a train, and crossed the length of France.

comments.name: Hari Prasad
comments.body: After years of study of the neuroscience, phenomenology and psychology of consciousness, it seems helpful to consider different types of awareness and agency normally subsumed by the word.  At the physical level sensations and reactions come first, with emotional identity forming through mirroring and shared emotional resonance with a parent or care giver.  Language, words, thoughts, concepts come later.  There can be no conscious (verbal) memories from before that stage.  There can be continuity of personality (emotional coloring, pitch, tonality) from before then, the preverbal stage.

Awareness isn’t consciousness. An insect is aware of it's environment.

Consciousness is an awareness that you have an individual identity separate from your environment and that you have agency relative to it.

Your dog is conscious. It's not the same level of consciousness as yourself but it's there.

The question of whether AI is conscious is interesting if it ever were placed in a physical body. But whether they should be regulated would be the same as should there be regulations on the behavior of your dog or yourself in relation to it.

Most people only have really foggy notions if complex philosophical, ethical and legal issues.

Animal fetuses too, such as birds still in the egg starting to recognize the mother's song, and some shark and antelope fetuses killing each other in utero.  How can a fetus floating in the dark with such limited experience have any understanding in a self aware, conscious way? None of us remember birth or early infancy, such as where kids don't know they were adopted if it happened early on.  My earliest documented memory is at 2 years old.  Don't go beyond your data and confuse people, such as those who will no doubt use this to limit women's access to abortions.

comments.name: John
comments.body:
I wish there was some mention of the dominant definition  in the philosophical and social discourse on this topic - phenomenal consciousness. Is there any feeling, or subjective sense of what it’s like to be a baby? This is what Michael Pollan is writing popular books about. This is what the AI conversation is about. AI is already self aware. It knows it exists. It can speculate on what’s going on under the hood. Not a big deal. But is there any subjectivity? Could it suffer? If so, moral concerns apply. 

The hard problem of consciousness is not self awareness. Not whatever this article is about. It’s subjective experience. If a baby can feel pain it’s conscious. If it’s just reflexes it’s not. I don’t think anyone seriously doubts a baby can’t feel pain. Articles like this just muddy the waters unfortunately by not understanding the terms of the debate.

58. How do humans create genuinely new concepts — not just random variations or recombinations of old ideas?
Alison Gopnik, cognitive scientist, University of California, Berkeley

I think you are asking, how do humans create original works? Original works are works that originate a new or different way of seeing the world around us. Picasso’s “Les demoiselles d’Avignon” is a work that opens up a new way of seeing paintings. Mondrian’s works do the same. Einstein’s theory of relativity opens up a new way of understanding our world. Darwin’s The Origin of the Species does the same. E. O. Wilson’s experiment with ants opened up our understanding of how ants communicate. James Joyce’s Ulysses invented a new way of writing novels. Ramón Lull invented the new language, Catalan. Sir Arthur Fleming discovered penicillin. All these instances indicate the appearance of something that ushers a new or different way of looking at things. They originate a new perspective or use. Now, what empowers the originator to achieve this new outlook? The imagination. The human imagination is the capacity to see how things can not be what they are. Sartre’s work, Imagination (1936), is the best description of this capacity I know. He calls it the capacity to nihilate: seeing that a thing or situation does NOT have to be what it is but can be something else. This is the sine qua non of originality.

As a therapist, a few things that drive me crazy: 

People who “are” their diagnoses, as in “I’m OCD” or I’m ADD”. 

Clinicians who refer to their patients as their diagnosis, as in “he’s a schizophrenic”. 

Critics who deny a role for diagnosis, as if all mental health problems were non existent or are the same. 

Insurance companies who refer to us as “providers”, emphasizing our role in the structure of the administrative system, rather than our role as helpers. 

I also hated when we went from “mental health” to “behavioral health”. 

Clinicians who have an allegiance to a specific school of therapy rather than an allegiance to the patient. 

(I prefer the term “patient” to “client”, even if it reifies the medical model. “Patient” refers to the person’s suffering. “Client” refers to the contractual relationship.) 

Life is more complex than mere diagnosis, but defining the problem is a step toward addressing it. 

BTW, in my experience, the biggest missed diagnoses are substance use disorders. Without carefully assessing the substance use of a patient, it’s easy to overdiagnose psychopathology, prescribe meds and psychological treatment, when what the patient needs is a referral to AA or SMART Recovery.

Data entry, validation, audit, identifying exceptions/risks/outliers... The private sector is already using AI tools for this and seeing better results at lower costs. It's absolutely something the public sector should leverage. 
2 - AI is not a person. Stop conflating all of the nonsense about sentience and biases and all the other headline grabbing nonsense with the potential to make poorly managed, manual processes work better.

Guyyyyssss. Everyone. Listen. Cats won't eat anything that doesn't smell like food to them. They "eat with their noses" the same way humans "eat with their eyes". Snotty noses, cold pate, or stale kibble will all be detrimental to a cat's appetite.

Store kibble in an airtight reclosable bag and squeeze the air out of it every time you close it. For larger bags of kibble, consider putting a portion (like a week's worth) into a smaller bag for daily use, limiting the air exposure to the bulk of the kibble. 

Microwave canned food if you can, especially if it's been in the fridge. Just 5-15 seconds is usually enough, then stir. Ideally you want it at "mouse body temperature" (100-103F)
You can also pour some hot water into a larger bowl and set the can or bowl of food in or on top of the hot water for a few minutes. If the water cools before the food is warm, dump out the water and replace with more hot water.
A lot of the flavor is in the gravy/juices that stick to the can, and even plain pate has a little of it. Put a little hot water in the can and stir or swirl it to deglaze the can, then pour it into the dish with the food to boost the aroma.

comments.body: I think something needs to be clarified here, and I’m only at the second paragraph. It’s not “an election commission appointed by Prime Minister Modi”, but the Election Commission of India, a constitutional body, whose members are appointed by the President of India. Initially the ECI was a one member (aka the Chief Election Commissioner) led body, after which in 1993 they changed it to a three member led body. Until 2023, these appointments were made on the advice of the Prime Minister and the rest of the Cabinet. In March 2023, in a landmark judgement in Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court stated that leaving the appointments to the executive branch compromised the independence of the elections and the independence of the ECI as envisaged in the Constitution. The Supreme Court ruled that the Parliament needs to enact a formal law regarding a Selection Committee that would advise the President on Election Commissioner appointments, and till such time that a law was passed, an ad hoc three member committee was to be formed consisting of the Prime Minister, The Chief Justice of India, and the Leader of the Opposition. In December of 2023, the Modi Government introduced a law about this Selection Committee, and explicitly removed the Chief Justice of India from the Committee and added in a Union Cabinet Minister (which would make any recommendation default to 2-1 in favour of the PM’s candidate) and quashing any sense of neutrality that the Supreme Court sought.

His 1890 book is “The Influence of Sea Power Upon History, 1660 – 1783.” 

Available on Amazon, paperback $15.99, hardcover $23.65.

Trump has single-handedly created the effects of an artificial “peak oil” crisis. Scholars of the theory  should take note for when the authentic threat eventually arrives? 

After the oil shocks of the 1970s, geologist M. King Hubbert and others predicted that global crude oil production would reach a maximum rate and then enter terminal decline. The effects would be skyrocketing fuel and energy prices, supply chain failure, recessions and geopolitical conflict, among others. 

The prediction was delayed by technological innovations like fracking, green technology and electric vehicles. Today, however, Trump has artificially created the conditions for a peak oil crisis.

First, he foolishly eliminated the Biden's wise investments in clean power generation and electric vehicles. Second, he followed Israel into a needless war without considering that Iran would respond by shutting down oil transportation in the Gulf. 

Now, absent a negotiated settlement acceptable to Iran, Trump's peak oil crisis will trigger a recession, “stagflation,” and political unrest at home and severe crises and hunger abroad. 

Rather than wait on Trump, the Gulf States and oil companies should devise a financial package to help Iran rebuild in return for reopening the Straits?

comments.name: Norman

We regularly get VAT refunded when we leave Europe. 

We have never been asked to show our purchases. Indeed,  when leaving Nice, France Airport there is a bank of machines where you can scan the barcode on the special form.
ALWAYS ask for your refund to your credit or debit card to avoid even more fees.

We create a spreadsheet of the refunds we expect and a copy of the refund form until we get it.

Note, Global Blue charges a high fee out of your refund. 
If the VAT rate is 20% you will likely get about 10-11% refunded.

comments.body:
Kingsolver has illuminated one of the great elements of life: How little things we do for others may make a monumental difference in their lives.

I am reminded of the parable of the philosopher and her student walking the beach and encountering a numberless school of grounded fish struggling to regain the water.
She picks up one fish and throws it back into its home in the sea. Her companion chides her for making the obviously meaningless gesture of saving one fish out of millions. 
She replies: It means everything to that one fish.
Something to keep in mind as we all struggle through the cluttered. emotional minefield. Kingsolver knows wherefrom she writes.

Throughout Europe, Scandinavia and Mexico, artists' houses and studios are preserved.  Tour groups troop through.  There is an atmosphere filled with clues about the artist's life and energy are part of these house/studio museums. And sometimes, maybe one in a thousand, a visitor sees something that lights a spark and they go back to their studio to make art.

Bob bought Captiva because an astrologer told him to.  In other words, it was divinely destined and the stars aligned.

Bob's house on Lafayette is an essential element of who he was.  Unless one spent time in the house, it is probably difficult to most people to imagine how scruffy and Rauschenbergian the neighborhood was and how the house was the essence of Bob's time and place.  

If they need more space, Bob left millions and millions and millions of dollars worth of work that could buy dozens of spaces for art related activities.

I, for one, will miss the aura of Bob's presence if the building is sold and sanitized by its new owners, erasing his presence and spirit.

Does the estate, now worth almost half a billion dollars really need the money from the sale of the building? 

As Joni Mitchell sagely sang, "...you don't know what you've got 'til it's gone".

comments.name: Scaramouche
comments.body:
Gordon Davis was the kind of Commissioner and boss that everyone would want to have. Exceptionally kind and aware, he understood and appreciated human nature and the foibles as well as the every day courage that employees demonstrated. 

I was very fortunate to Commissioner Davis, as I always enjoyed calling him when I would run into him after he had left the Parks Department over the years.
He would always have that kind, wry smile in response and ask how I was doing and offer some advice. 

He hired me in 1980 and started me on a long career at Parks. It was through his creativity and intelligence that the modern Parks Department was created in a time of severe budget restrictions after the city’s fiscal crisis.  Concessioning 13 golf courses so that golf professionals would administer and upgrade them instead of park workers who didn’t have that special expertise that was badly needed. 

He reintroduction of the borough commissioners that gave each borough executive level management further down into the organization that provided better management and more intelligent community and political outreach efforts that increased support for parks. 

Commissioner Davis created the Urban Park Rangers and the Parks Enforcement Patrol that allowed the Parks Department to better manage the many special events that had not been well-regulated before him and that held engender respect for parks by the general public as well.  He cared about his employees and he fought for them.

In Northern California, we've always looked at Alaska as the only place where the salmon system was naturally working, but that harvest H is now problematic and out of balance in the face of increasingly rapid climate change.  Pulling out the dams on the Klamath and the rapid recolonization by salmon afterwards gives us hope, but only if the commercial take is limited.  Increasing water temperatures compromise necessary cold water habitat for salmon and hatcheries both provide juveniles and pollute the gene pools of specific runs.

comments.body: While some continue to criticize our president for defunding AI research and other cutting-edge technologies, he has merely offered scientists the newfound freedom to decamp to other authoritarian destinations. In 2025, the Trump administration canceled or suspended more than 7,800 NIH and NSF grants, leaving roughly 2,600 projects—and $1.4 billion in unspent research funding—still unrestored by early 2026. The NIH awarded 22% fewer new grants overall (and 24% fewer flagship R01 grants) than its previous ten-year average, while the NSF awarded 25% fewer, an impressively efficient way to ensure tomorrow’s discoveries happen somewhere other than America. Trump also proposed cutting NIH funding by about $18 billion, or 40%, NSF funding by 57%, and NASA’s science directorate by 47%—because apparently the surest route to American scientific greatness is guaranteeing that cutting-edge breakthroughs occur in China. Many of these Chinese studied in the US and began work there before the Trump era.  To present an accurate picture, you have to study the international movement of scientists over the past several years, which this article fails to do.  I suspect the idea that America is an attractive destination while China is not predates the present global situation.  

Further, the number of elite Chinese workers in the US has decreased, while the number of Chinese workers trained in China is increasing.  

A Stanford study on. DeepSeek indicated that of 223 authors of technical papers nearly all had been educated or trained in China; more than half had never left China at all,  and of the roughly quarter who had some US experience, most later returned to China. 
      In short, the previous huge imbalance is gradually reversing partly because of Trump policies and US chauvinism, and partially because of China's growing expertise and support for scientists, regardless of ethnicity or nationality.

From the golden era of Def Jam Recordings to dominant runs on network television and the silver screen, LL Cool J set the blueprint for longevity and versatility in hip-hop. Few artists have evolved so seamlessly from raw street lyricism to global icon status while maintaining their undisputed legacy.

​Before the worldwide acclaim, however, the bedrock was laid in Hollis, Queens. Run-DMC and the late, legendary Jam Master Jay kicked down doors, brought rap into mainstream rock-and-roll consciousness, and put their neighborhood firmly on the cultural map.

​Architecting it all behind the scenes was Russell Simmons, whose vision, instinct, and unwavering belief transformed hip-hop from a regional subculture into a dominant global force.

With the completion of the Hollis LIRR station rebuild, the MTA has a timely opportunity to honor local history. I have been requesting that the MTA rename or co-name the station to commemorate Hollis's legendary hip-hop pioneers, such as Run-DMC and LL Cool J (e.g., Hollis – Run-DMC Station or Hollis – Hip-Hop Heritage Station).

Hollis is world-famous as the launching pad for hip-hop royalty. Recognizing these hometown icons at their neighborhood station would serve as a lasting tribute to Queens's global cultural influence and a tremendous source of pride for local residents.

comments.name: R
comments.body:
I really wish excessive noise in residential neighborhoods was taken more seriously. It's New York City, so no I don't expect silence. However, it seems to be getting worse and sometimes you can't even pinpoint the origin.    There's no reason to play music so loud that I feel the vibration in my apartment or my phone instantly identifies the song even when my windows are closed.

The effect on hearing, sleep and overall stress can be significant. On the other hand, I do understand the concerns about privacy. Not too long ago, the NYT had an article about noise detectors in a public housing development somewhere in New England. The use of the detectors was very creepy and Orwellian.

comments.name: geoff
comments.body:
I can understand the reservations about noise cameras: i.e., they can turn us all into characters in Coppola's film [The Conversation].

On the other hand, living in Jackson Heights for the last twenty-five years, I continue to be astonished at how unconstrained is (1) gratuitous honking -- honking that alters nothing about the traffic situation -- and (2) loud music from cars every weekend. (Consider yourself very lucky if your apartment is not on a corner with a stoplight.)

It becomes, then defines, the normal and nothing will move that needle because there is no enforcement. One could wait forever if waiting for the 115 Pct to issue a ticket on 37th Avenue or Roosevelt Avenue. And the NYPD could give out a month's worth of citations on any given weekend.

comments.name: Rebecca
comments.body: Man, I *wish* my neighborhood had noise-detecting cameras. People just *love* to drive through my neighborhood blasting music (where the bass is so extreme I can feel it inside my apartment) or revving their engines or whatever (where it's easy to make assumptions about what the driver's insecure about). It's obnoxious and the people who do it know it's unlikely they'll get caught in the act.

comments.name: Juswhipped
comments.body: Some of us in areas like Mount Vernon,   Yonkers,  New Rochelle  who live along parkway and interstate have been waiting for the noise cameras.  Maybe the more city folk move our way they will pay attention to the noise we are subjected to like they do in NYC. Sorry can't feel sorry for NYC folk and I grew up in NYC

comments.name: Joe Dokes
comments.body:
As for Mr. Aquilino, he needs to understand that the rules apply to everyone, not just the poor and middle classes. 
They instruct those who don't understand the need for civil behavior - even if they can afford a $275,000 car. 
Or especially, in his case.

comments.name: Joe Dokes
comments.body:
Noise is a serious problem that the city needs to take seriously at the highest levels. 
It comes down to a basic issue of thinking of others, which is essential for urban life. 
For whatever reason, some people don't get this. They toss trash, they blow through red lights - and they make excessive noise.
A first step would be telling them this is harmful behavior; the next step is punishment. It's as simple as that. 
Basic anti-social behaviors - tossing food wrappers, putting feet on public seats, spitting gum on the sidewalk, aggressive driving - need to stop. Really. 
There is no reason NYC can't be as clean, safe, quiet, polite, and comfortable as other major cities. The only difference is enforcement and leadership.

comments.name: NYCGal

According to this NYC has a camera problem. Well not in my neighborhood Astoria! 

I have written to the DOT a number of times to add cameras on 31st street under the train, and on the corners of 31st Street and 31st Avenue where a massive bike lane was added last year.  

The things I see a few times a week I pass there early in the morning, would make the city so much money. 

So many drivers run the red light, so many drivers park in the bike path, so many drivers park illegally, or conduct illegal activities in these zones, that you’d think it would be ripe for some city revenue in the form of fines!!!

comments.name: NokoMarie
comments.body: The administration's dismantling of the CDC and NIH as recently reported in this paper are real cause for alarm here and abroad. They both played a major role in treating Ebola as well as fighting it through research and boots on the ground treatment in Africa. In a world of air travel, this one infected passenger is all it takes to spread this horrific disease, as well as others, internationally. Secretary Kennedy and his boss are frightfully ignorant of the consequences. As if this was not enough, now we have to worry about a plague outbreak in Russia a country with zero transparency. Praying that we will see science and pursuit of knowledge restored to their rightful places come 2028 if the Democrats prevail in the midterms.

comments.name: George
comments.body:
The very first think Kenyan authorities need to do is find out who else was on the flight the victim took from Uganda to Kenya.

The fact that he drove from Congo to Uganda despite the latter's border controls is troublesome enough.  But that he could then board a flight from Uganda to Kenya shows that containment of the Ebola contagion is fraught with "holes".

Equally worrisome is the fact that Kenya, far more than either Congo or Uganda, is a major foreign tourist destination.  Kenya's economy is dependent to a considerable degree on tourism; particularly from Europe, but also North America.

On a larger basis, it is essential that efforts be increased to find both a cure for Ebola and a preventative vaccine if that is at all possible.  An effort that will likely need to take place outside the US given the massive defunding of America's CDC and consequent unscientific embracing of anti-vax ideology.

comments.name: Emma
comments.body: I understand the desire to get better medical care, but in the process of evading border controls, the deceased selfishly and unnecessarily exposed hundreds of innocent bystanders on his flight to Nairobi, at the two airports involved, and on his journey from the DRC to Uganda, a border that is purportedly closed, all while very ill (since he went directly from the airport to a Nairobi hospital). One hopes that this doesn't turn into another epidemic.

comments.name: Blanche White
comments.body:
With hopes for Kenya to be spared what these people selfishly brought to them after experiencing health problems in a place with an outbreak of Ebola.

This man, who had been sick for a month, and his relatives went to great lengths to get back to Kenya, via Uganda from the Congo where he had been for seven years.

If he went by road to Uganda, he still boarded a plane to Kenya and there, at least, is where the group should have been caught if protocols were in place.

It is sad for this man, who wanted to live, and his relatives, also in harm's way, but my heart is tempered for all those they chose to endanger along their way.

comments.name: Science Teacher
comments.body: Thousands have died - what are we doing to assist?  if this were happening in Europe, what would be the reaction?  But it's Africa, so..?

comments.name: Nora
comments.body: "The man had traveled by road to Uganda and then took a flight to Nairobi, the Kenyan capital, on Saturday, Mr. Duale said." Sorry - what!? The man with an active Ebola infection boarded an international flight? How was this allowed to happen?

comments.name: Marcus
comments.body: Why would he hop on a plane and knowingly put other passengers in danger if he knew he was sick?

comments.name: MW
comments.body: Are we reading this correctly?  An obviously very ill man from the Congo (where Ebola is spreading) was able to fly into Kenya, so sick he was taken directly to a hospital, and no one intervened?  Where was Kenya’s border control, airline personnel?  And what about the people who assisted him with this mad journey?  Now an entire Nation faces this crisis because nobody had the courage to say “no?”  Are we looking at corruption or stupidity?

comments.body:
Algorithmic Acquiescence in the Age of AI

Over-reliance on automated decision systems often induces automation bias, where human operators yield in passive acquiescence to erroneous model predictions rather than verifying the raw telemetry or auditing the latent feature attributions. This uncritical compliance undermines effective human-in-the-loop oversight, turning what should be a robust verification checkpoint into mere rubber-stamping.

comments.name: Keith Barnes

comments.name: Michael Rowley
comments.body:
A Requiem for Q

We gather in quiet quarters to record the obsequies of a queenly character, our questionable and quaint companion, the letter Q. 

You brought a certain ‘je ne sais quoi,’ a unique mystique, and a picturesque status to our prose.

Under close critique, we see your masquerade. You are a linguistic quack, an antiquarian holdover demanding an obsequious ’U’ to follow your every whim.

Rest in peace, Dear Q— 
No! No! Do not go! I cannot quit you!

Daily, I submit to your quotidian joys. I shall forever surrender my unrequited affections in quiet acquiescence.

XO,
Frank

comments.name: Keith Barnes
comments.body: Messi's messianic presence on the field has usually induced humble acquiescence in the opposition, but now he's retired his evanescence will be a thing of the past, not made to last live, surviving only when replays are revived.

comments.name: Keith Barnes
comments.body: We've gradually abandoned our feeble acquiescence to planned obsolescence, seeking lasting qualities. Detroit exploited it, making small annual changes to their styling excrescences, to persuade car owners to buy the latest model for display on their driveway, one up on their neighbors as a reward for their labors.

comments.body: Fauci is an icon - he served our nation very well. His brilliance, courage and scientific acumen are outstanding. America is proud of him for his services and contributions. It is a shame that quacks supported by corrupt officials are trying to destroy the man who gave his life for us. It is a political game to earn media exposure for them. Alas, they are morally bankrupt. They are making a mockery of the media. Social media highlights the quacks as their hatred makes sensational news. Dr. Fauci - hang in there. Most Americans are with you.

comments.name: ManhattanWilliam
comments.body:
In spite of his many flaws, Larry Kramer has always been a hero of mine because while gay men were dying by the thousands and being ignored by all levels of our government, he was out there getting people motivated to fight for money and research and medicine that no doubt led to some people living who might otherwise have died.  

I remember the period well.  As a gay man, I was more terrified of being stigmatized and driven to isolation if I contracted the fatal disease than actually getting sick itself.  The image of family and friends having to come visit me while wearing head-to-toe protective clothing was a nightmare, not to mention that even mothers were afraid to kiss or even hug their dying sons in spite of reassurances that neither act was dangerous.  

The strange relationship that developed between Kramer and Fauci absolutely led to lives being saved, making my feelings towards them one of great admiration above all else.  When people choose to criticize either of these men for actions that they might find distasteful looking back retrospectively, I ask the simple question: when Larry Kramer was out there marching to save people's lives by having them recognized as human beings whom society had totally ostracized and while Fauci was pushing to get drugs approved at breakneck speed, what were the rest of doing?  These 2 men saved  thousands of lives.  I have not nor will I ever forget their tenacity, anger, and desire to help those that everyone else had cast off.

comments.name: Vince
comments.body:
Sorry, I hated, hated, hated the staging.  And I was not alone.
.

comments.name: Chad
comments.body: I cannot agree with the sentiment that this was well directed. The acting was great - but the staging, to me, felt like someone decided to just throw their coke-induced fever dream onto stage, call it 'art,' and dare you to question it. Pre-show you sit with a wall of blinding stage lights blasting at you. The caller is first on roller blades, then a giant inflatable chicken costume, then a sweater - for no discernible reason. They take 5 minute (I timed it) of nothing happening but a foam machine filling the stage, and then the action continues without so much as a nod to it until Kramer squeegees it around at the end. Whatever symbolism arguments one wants to make, I just do not buy. Moreover, I take issue with St. Ann's Warehouse stating in multiple places "starting promptly, no late seating," and then seating late comers at the show I attended.

comments.name: MichaelM
comments.body: Overall I enjoyed the show with strong performances across the board. I was less of fan of the staging which felt gimmicky and distracting.

comments.name: Paul Barnes
comments.body: I'm familiar with Daniel Fish's work from his days on the west coast - San Francisco Bay Area and Shakespeare Santa Cruz, most specifically. He is one of the most daring, inventive, and iconoclastic directors working in the American theatre, and though already widely recognized for his revival of "Oklahoma!" and other productions east of the Sierra Nevada, I'm glad to know he's continuing to push boundaries and envelopes in New York City - especially as we still do battle with another plague that has taken countless lives and is likely to rear its ugly, lethal head again. Kramer and Fauci are great Americans. Not without their flaws; both helping us thread our way through the unimaginable, each in his own way, with their own calm/ferocious voices. Not gods; just humans tasked with formidable challenges, fueled by their compassion and concern. I haven't seen Fauci/Kramer, but it is apparent that once again, the theatre holds the mirror up so we may see ourselves and the world in which we live reflected back - even, or especially, on a stage covered in foam.

comments.name: Karen
comments.body: This tragic story can happen to ANY family no matter whether there are two parents, financial security, top schools, etc. My deepest sympathies to the Gerber family and others that are struggling. We were fortunate that when our teen went through something like this18 years ago, the wildnessness and therapeutic boarding school programs worked the first time. Both programs were excellent, nuturing and privately, not corporate, owned. We are happy and grateful for our child and our family today. As an employed, married adult, our child has several good long-time friends from that school who have also done well. Be kind to people who struggle, you have no idea what they may have been through and whether or not you may be next.

comments.name: Annie
comments.body: My heart goes out to his family, and especially his sister who seems like a truly nice person and a real supporter of her brother. Her recent comments about him were super empathic, clearly said with deep love and respect.

comments.name: nancy
comments.body:
What an absolute heartbreak for everyone in his life.

It seems that children of the famous have a very difficult time growing up under their parents' spotlight, figuring out who THEY are, and what THEY can be and do of value, outside of their famous parents. We see it over and over again.

Isn't that one of the reasons these children may often develop anxieties, insecurities, vulnerability to drugs etc, because of a lack of personal goals to work towards, and a lack of a solid self image and worth, without* their famous parents, and all that affords them.
Why don't famous parents encourage their children to explore other interests, other than go in to show business, modeling, etc? Why don't they encourage them to develop their own identities, interests and careers, become scientists, teachers, doctors, trades people, builders, go in to service oriented jobs, etc, ...any number of other valuable professions, where they can be their own person and not be constantly compared to their parents, constantly under a spotlight they never asked for?  

Young adults need to have something to work toward, to feel capable of managing their own lives, and know that they can work hard and overcome obstacles..without being under a spotlight.

comments.name: CC
comments.body: These tragic deaths are difficult to understand. At one time, I might have had a comment or two about ways he could have been helped, especially as a young man with so many resources and clearly loving parents. But I lost my own step-son at 27 from an overdose, after years of expensive rehab and the continued faith of his father, a beloved doctor in the community. Addiction and mental illness do not recognize any social stratum. In both cases, everything that could have been done was done. The Gerbers are suffering. I only hope they take comfort knowing their son struggled valiantly against twin monsters, and tried to help others in the same fight. His life had meaning - his death may prevent others. May his memories be a blessing.

comments.name: marin
comments.body: I wish nothing but the best for the Gerber family. At 27 he was an adult and though I've seen some media outlets suggesting there was a problem in the Gerber household but I think it's very speculative and hurtful  to make such assumptions. Presley might have been characterologically or genetically more at risk for depression etc. His sister seems to be doing good by all accounts. Children from the same family can also experience their childhood very differently, because of differences in character, life experiences and place within the family. I'm sure every parent of a troubled child wil already feel guilt after the untimely and preventable death of that child, without outsiders piling on.

A small amount, .5 to 1.5 mg. caused mania and fear in someone who has a low tolerance and the near cancellation of an annual trip abroad. Once I stopped the use of the smallest amount of lorazepam I began to stop feeling manic and fearful. The amount I was prescribed is small according to what I read, but it caused me despair. My heart goes out to Presley Gerber after reading what he went through and his family, too, of course. My benzo experience showed how seductive and hurtful it can be even at my low level of use.

Nelson Mandela famously said "If you talk to a man in a language he understands, that goes to his head. If you talk to him in his language, that goes to his heart."

Watching people's faces brighten and their hearts open when Yuji speaks a few words in their language is a beautiful thing. Speaking someone else's language shifts the power dynamic and breaks down barriers.

I've experienced this when I use my French to connect with immigrants in my area. I've received comments like "we need more of this" from fellow passengers on the bus who've overheard our conversations. I have to agree--if more Americans spoke at least one other language, more bridges would be built. I've just started learning Spanish and find even a few words can make a difference.

If polyglot content creators can inspire us to build connections by speaking to others in a language that goes to their heart, more power to them.

Which is kind of wild since English itself is a fusion of Germanic and Romance roots, with hefty infusions of vocabulary from other languages, including Spanish, Italian, Yiddish, Arabic, Hindi, and native American languages, as well as Latin and Greek.

comments.name: bill strong
comments.body:
It's a recent US tragedy that a second language is difficult for some, impossible for most.  Millions of Americans' recent ancestors spoke two or three languages from early childhood.
Recently I've taught English to Afghan teenagers who were quickly studies, in part b/c they already spoke Dari, Pashto, Hindi, understood Farsi, Tajiki, Urdu and Arabic - English was just one more.  I took one illiterate and fearful adult aunt to the doctor.  She was afraid and I couldn't communicate with her.  The Indian receptionist asked me her native language and soon they were happily chatting in Farsi/Dari after trying Hindi and switching.  Several of the teenagers now live in Ontario and are learning French.  They switch languages in conversation with ease.
US schools decided to start world languages at age 13 - the stupidest age to start and to teach with textbooks.  To my good fortune my French teacher led 30 of us on a 4-month sound odyssey w/o any print material - just child-like chatter for a few weeks, by Dec.r conversation on simple subjects. In Jan. we began to look at words and read simple paragraphs.  60 years later my 3 years of French lives on in my brain and occasionally from my mouth.  HS Latin and college German, taught w/ books from the start, are mere fossils.  
Anybody remember the story of Sacajawea - Lewis and Clark's guide/interpreter?  Several indigenous languages &  Eng&Fr.  Most ancient people knew their own language and the languages of several neighbors.

comments.name: Richard C. Gross
comments.body: I'm sorry to see many negative comments about what these people think robots will hold in store for us. I believe they could help give us a magnificent future, especially once the technology evolves to the point of giving us humanoid androids.

comments.name: Cassandra Kavanagh
comments.body: Unfortunately, social isolation and the accompanying emotional distress and mental health issues are on the rise. Despite being designed as social animals, our species now struggles to connect, and this sort of technology will only increase the divide. Over 100's of thousands of years ago, human beings evolved to be co-operative hunter-gatherers connected to each other and the living earth. Rituals, song, dance, art, and storytelling made us the creature we are in a time when mutual aid was essential to survival ...Humanity was doomed to suffer when we moved towards agriculture and a class system where the world's poor work to create wealth for the elite. This trajectory eventually resulted in the Industrial Revolution that propelled us with brute force towards a present that is so far removed from our hunter-gatherer past that our psyche and souls can't deal with it.  We may think we are ready, but we are not. We have not evolved for the world we are creating.

comments.name: Catherine

Lot's of people stood to benefit turning the instinct to help, the 'water brigade', where each of us does what we can to deal with something bigger than any one of us could deal with alone, into a firestorm, making everything more dangerous for everyone.

News became an enemy, truth became an enemy.  Instead of a shared knowledge with facts that were accepted and embraced as the reality of our lives.

With the introduction of AI, and its ability to conduct violence free of human intervention, a whole new layer of disintergration is being set to become unleashed into our lives.

We need to be able to step back, and take a look at the big picture of what we are turning into here in this nation, and what our neighbors across the planet are also becoming.

The urge to help, the need to be human, is being overwhelmed by another instinct, the fear of 'other'.  On a planet as small as ours, the problem of avoiding violence is that we have been taught that everyone not us is 'other'.

It was an annual tradition to take the apple harvest every year to a centuries-old water mill, crush the fruit, and then begin the process of fermenting the juice into hard cider (Moscht). During the winter months, a glass of Moscht was a staple during the evening meal. Everyone had a barrel in the garage or basement. This inspired me earlier this year to start making it in our own home, where we now have it available most of the time. It is incredibly easy, inexpensive, and the results are astoundingly good. I guess I can credit Mr. Watson for inspiring all the online videos I consulted prior to making the first batch, so my hat's off to him. Condolences to his friends and family.

In essence, American politics increasingly center less on the practical consequences of government policies and more on abstract, emotions driven arguments in the midst of great societal changes like “artificial intelligence and the war in Gaza” (New York Times) which signal allegiance to a particular party’s ideology. This evolution is most clearly seen in the shift from reasonable policy disagreement between political opponents to the rejection of an opponent’s legitimacy. In the era of consensus, (which by that I really mean the post war period) electoral defeat was more commonly understood as an unfortunate, yet legitimate outcome, and the representative of the opposing party was seen as another American, albeit with different views. Now, as populist rhetoric intensifies these divisions, electoral defeat can become an existential threat, and the opposing candidate is portrayed as a public enemy who threatens the existence of the community. I believe we, as Americans, should understand the true threat to the sacred role of democracy in this nation lies in presenting one political camp as the sole or authentic representative of the people.
